title: Texas Trailblazers and the Hard Truth About AI in Legal Work
author: Greg Lambert · Marlene Gebauer

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source identifies rapid learning needs for vendors and law firms and proposes discussion of buyer expectations and platform competition, which is adjacent to the cluster’s emphasis on organisational readiness and control of the working environment. However, it primarily promotes conferences and provides no evidence or clear position on whether product expansion exceeds realised value, workflow fit, renewal economics or consumption costs.
qs: This, as you know, is a time when people are still learning  And there’s so much happening every single day.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s framing of AI adoption as an organisational design problem rather than simple lawyer substitution, and materially extends it by proposing human review embedded in governance and by identifying compensation and billing targets as implementation incentives. It does not, however, provide evidence that automation has already weakened the expertise or partner-succession pipeline.
qs: They incorporate it into their governance plans that there is always human review.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core copilot proposition: AI capability is uneven, legal work remains human-led, and verification must be embedded in redesigned workflows. It materially extends the synthesis by showing how billable-hour incentives, associate targets, client pricing preferences and organisational readiness can enable or obstruct implementation.
qs: But our culture and our businesses and just the way that we’re structured, there’s a huge gulf between what’s possible and what’s doable.
Everything is AI assisted, not AI done completely.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that AI challenges production economics more than the continuing role of lawyers. It specifically reinforces the conflict between AI-enabled efficiency and hourly billing, while acknowledging that hourly pricing will remain suitable for some work, and identifies compensation and billing targets as barriers to adoption.
qs: It’s like one of the things I said on the panel I was on was like, know, AI doesn’t kill the billable hour, but it does expose its limits.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: Shaver supports the cluster’s core view that a rapidly changing legal-technology market creates continuing learning and information needs. She reinforces the vendor-facing side of the cluster’s prescription by presenting dedicated education on buyer expectations, investment and selling to law firms, but offers no evidence on product growth, adoption, revenue or performance.
qs: This, as you know, is a time when people are still learning  And there’s so much happening every single day.

kp.k: Human verification must be built into AI workflows
kp.d: Reporting Ron McNamee’s introduction of “cognitive surrender,” Lambert describes users overtrusting AI and accepting its answers rather than checking them. Gebauer recommends incorporating human review into workflow design, governance and education, with responsible personnel identifying the stages requiring review. These are practitioner observations and recommendations, not measured findings about reliance.
qs: it’s basically where you are over trusting the AI and you’re offloading that cognitive load to the AI.
They incorporate it into their governance plans that there is always human review. Everything is AI assisted, not AI done completely.

kp.k: Billing incentives can undermine associate AI adoption
kp.d: Lambert reports conference discussions about how partner compensation and associate billing targets may accelerate or obstruct adoption. He presents the possibility of AI removing 50% of associate work as an incentive problem being discussed, not an established displacement estimate. Gebauer argues that efficiency conflicts with hourly revenue incentives and that innovation-hour credits do not fully resolve that conflict. Associate hiring reductions are raised as a question, without a reported decision or forecast.
qs: how partner compensation and associated billing targets either accelerate or kill AI adoption?
this can take 50 % of the associate’s work away, what’s the incentive for them to do this?
AI doesn’t kill the billable hour, but it does expose its limits.

kp.k: AI shifts pricing debates from speed to value
kp.d: Lambert attributes to Kyle Poe of Legora a proposed shift in 2026 from tool speed toward pricing the value of AI-assisted work. Poe reportedly hears firms seeking flat fees that reward efficiency while some clients prefer hourly billing to capture reduced hours. Gebauer recommends explicit client–firm discussions about whether value means time, outcomes, faster insights or earlier resolution; no settled pricing model is reported.
qs: how do we price this new value that we’re setting up?
whoa, if it’s going to be less hours, maybe I just want to pay by the hour and I just pay you less.
the value is still there. It’s just the time that’s spent is less.

kp.k: Cheaper services may unlock previously uneconomic corporate work
kp.d: Lambert reports repeated conference references to a demand-expansion paradox: lower costs and shorter turnaround could release pent-up client demand. He treats this as a possibility and questions whether firms are preparing adequately. Gebauer also says in-house teams are considering tools to bring work back internally, making firms’ responses urgent. This concerns corporate legal demand and sourcing, not evidence of improved public access to justice.
qs: there’s a lot of pent up demand that I think clients would love for law firms to do more work for them, but the cost and time is prohibitive.
in-house groups are looking at tools that they can take some of this work back in.
I think it also opens up the opportunity to address work that just never got done because it just didn’t make economic sense.

kp.k: Client influence requires direct participation in transformation discussions
kp.d: Lambert contrasts conference claims about the power of general counsel and in-house lawyers with his observation that relatively few in-house attorneys attended the second day, despite substantial legal operations participation. Gebauer reports conflicting impressions of client AI maturity and seeks direct feedback. Their observations concern this event and do not establish general corporate adoption rates.
qs: there’s a lot of power in the hands of the in-house lawyers and general counsel of the clients.
There were not a lot of in-house attorneys that showed up for day two. It was a large crowd, but there were lots of legal ops people.
People are begging to hear from you. They want, really want direction.

kp.k: Software engineering analogies have limits for legal work
kp.d: The hosts report that Harvey’s general counsel compared lawyers with software engineers. They accept the shared problem-solving capabilities and the prospect of broader, technology-enabled roles, but reject a straightforward analogy between validating software outputs and judging legal services. They argue that negotiation, judges, juries and other external factors constrain legal outcomes. Claims that coding has been solved by AI are presented as industry assertions, not independently demonstrated findings.
qs: Agreed with the end result, but didn’t agree with the analysis. Yes.
the outputs that computer engineers have and the outputs that lawyers have, one can be independently validated for ⁓ correctness.
you’re also gonna have to be knowledgeable in one or two more areas, especially in using the technology that you have.
You have to understand the technology you’re using, all of those things.

kp.k: An AI-enabled survey reportedly halved a client’s price
kp.d: Lambert recounts Justin Schwartz’s example of asking outside counsel what a $10,000 multi-state survey would cost with AI; the reported price fell to $5,000. Counsel was reportedly surprised by permission to use AI because other clients prohibited it. The hosts frame this anecdote as evidence of the value of explicit client–firm conversations and suggest cheaper surveys could support more regular updates. The transcript provides no independent quality assessment or measured production time.
qs: if they used AI, what would a $10,000 multi-state survey cost?
the outside counsel was surprised that they were allowing them to use the AI to do this because other clients refused to let them do it.
it went from a $10,000 cost to a $5,000 cost.

kp.k: Large-scale extraction reportedly enabled previously impractical risk analysis
kp.d: Lambert recounts a Phillips 66 presentation about AI extraction from rights-of-way documents, recalling a volume of over 250,000 and reported savings well over a million dollars. He qualifies the savings interpretation by suggesting the work probably had not previously been performed because of cost. Gebauer adds that it may instead have occurred piecemeal as needed. The claimed benefit is broader visibility into information and risks, rather than clearly documented reductions in existing expenditure.
qs: over 250,000 of these that they had documents that explain what the rights away were.
he said it saved them well over a million dollars in cost to do that.
But the key thing was they probably didn’t even do it beforehand because the cost was so high.
not getting done or getting done piecemeal on an as need basis.

kp.k: Existing tools can support low-budget legal operations innovation
kp.d: Lambert reports that Elizabeth Poole of Boomi revamped an intake system using SharePoint and Co-Pilot with a stated budget of zero, calling it a vibe-coding example. The hosts use the anecdote to advocate curiosity and creative use of available tools. No quantified performance improvement or implementation evaluation is supplied.
qs: she developed a way of taking the intake system and revamping it using a combination of SharePoint and Co-Pilot
she said her budget to do this,  was zero.

kp.k: Reported fee trends show persistent hourly-model economics
kp.d: Lambert recounts a preview of a forthcoming Council Link report: AFAs remain at about 10%, while the reported blended measure of rate increases moved from around 3% before 2022 to 5% from about 2022 onward. The transcript does not specify the AFA denominator, sample or full methodology. Lambert himself characterizes the change as a 60% increase; that is his calculation, not a separately reported finding. The presenter’s suggestion that firms could seek to normalize 7% or more in two or three years is a prediction.
qs: here we are again right at about 10 % for AFAs.
before 2022 that on average the rates and this is a blended amount on how they measure it was around 3%.
She said about 2022 and after that has jumped to 5%.
if we could normalize 5%, you know, there’s gonna be a push to normalize 7 % or more

kp.k: Locally built AI tools create governance and complexity challenges
kp.d: Reporting a panel involving corporate participants, Lambert asks how organizations can govern individually created software without suppressing creativity. Gebauer raises approval-process questions for small practice-group or individual solutions and argues that complexity discourages adoption. Their discussion identifies an unresolved implementation problem rather than an established governance model.
qs: if we start allowing individuals to create their own software to correct their one problem that they’re facing, how do you manage that? How do you govern that?
as long as it’s complex, people don’t adopt it. If it’s easy, people do.

kp.k: Training must extend beyond operating AI tools
kp.d: Lambert reports Richard Gorlick’s warning about a possible “lawyer freak out of 2027,” treating substantial future change as anticipated rather than demonstrated. The hosts recommend early communication with affected personnel, transparent instruction about capabilities and limitations, governance guardrails, and cross-department sharing of scalable, repeatable use cases. Gebauer explicitly distinguishes this preparation from merely teaching tool operation.
qs: warning about the lawyer freak out of 2027.
if you’re not having those conversations now, when it is an emergency, it’s too late.
we have to teach people about what it does and doesn’t do.
We have to be sharing use cases

kp.k: Legal research remains difficult despite new vendor offerings
kp.d: Lambert reports Legora introducing a legal research option, revising his earlier expectation that providers such as Harvey and Legora would integrate research rather than pursue it themselves. The hosts describe research as particularly difficult and argue that access to case law alone does not meet the needs of practicing lawyers. These are product observations and practitioner judgments, not comparative performance results.
qs: Lagora is introducing a legal research option on their platform
legal research is really, really hard to do. It’s complicated and it’s hard to get right.
if legal research could be solved by just having the case law, then we’d all be using Google Scholar for all of our work.

kp.k: Verification must examine citation content as well as existence
kp.d: Discussing a Filevine presentation, the hosts stress that incorrect citations, quotations and analysis predate generative AI. They report disagreement and significant errors among established citators, but provide no study sample, methodology or numerical error rates. Gebauer asks how lawyers should verify both citation accuracy and substantive support when neither AI nor existing checking systems can simply be trusted. Lambert argues this reinforces the importance of skilled law librarians and vendor scrutiny.
qs: People were putting in wrong citations, bad citations, using the incorrect quotes and incorrect analysis. That is not an AI phenomenon.
they don’t agree and they have significant error
not only do have to check to make sure the citation is correct, you have to make sure that the content in the citation is correct.
it takes somebody really smart to keep on top of these vendors that think they’ve created the easy button for legal research.

kp.d: The hosts conclude that experimentation is proceeding without perfect clarity and recommend continued testing, horizon scanning and discussion. Lambert identifies culture, business arrangements and organizational structures as constraints separating AI’s technical possibilities from practical deployment. This is their overarching interpretation of the conference, not a quantified measure of adoption or productivity.
qs: nobody’s waiting for perfect clarity anymore. And that would be a mistake if you do
they’re not waiting for it to be perfect before they start testing it.
there’s a huge gulf between what’s possible and what’s doable.
the key right here is having these conversations now, working with the tools now.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI is changing workflows, pricing incentives, the scope of economically feasible work, professional skills and legal-technology markets, but the source distinguishes current examples from uncertain market-wide predictions.
pts.d: Greg Lambert describes overtrust and offloading judgment to AI as 'cognitive surrender', a term he reports Ron McNamee introduced at the conference. Marlene Gebauer argues for AI-assisted workflows with mandatory human verification rather than fully autonomous completion. She says AI efficiency exposes the limits of hourly billing and can discourage adoption when associates' billing targets and partners' compensation reward time spent. The suggestion that AI could remove 50% of associates' work is presented as something associates hear, not as a measured displacement finding. Lambert raises, rather than establishes, the possibility that cheaper legal services will unlock pent-up demand; Gebauer similarly predicts opportunities to perform previously uneconomic work. Neither supplies a definite associate-hiring forecast. Gebauer says in-house departments are exploring tools to take work back from firms. Kyle Poe of Legora, as reported by Lambert, predicts that the discussion from 2026 onward shifts from tool speed to pricing the resulting value; he reports competing preferences for firm-friendly flat fees and client-friendly hourly bills with fewer hours. Gebauer argues that value can remain despite reduced time and may include faster insights and resolution. Lambert predicts broader technological and interdisciplinary competence for lawyers; Gebauer says legal expertise alone is already insufficient. John LeBare of Harvey, as recounted by Lambert, compares lawyers and software engineers as producers of outputs. The hosts accept the broader skills implication but dispute the analogy's treatment of legal outcomes, which depend on negotiation and litigation contingencies. Reported practical examples include Justin Schwartz's outside counsel cutting the price of an AI-assisted multi-state survey from $10,000 to $5,000; Phillips 66 extracting information from a large rights-of-way document collection with claimed savings exceeding $1 million; and Elizabeth Poole at Boomi rebuilding intake with SharePoint and Co-Pilot on a stated zero budget. Christina Sikounis's Council Link presentation, as recounted by Lambert, describes persistent low AFA uptake and increasing fee-rate growth despite possible AI production efficiencies. Gebauer says complexity inhibits adoption, while individually built software creates governance questions. Richard Gorlick's reported 'lawyer freak out of 2027' warning anticipates substantial professional disruption without specifying its precise form. Harry St. John's reported presentation announces Legora's legal-research offering. Lambert and Gebauer emphasize that research remains difficult, citation problems predate generative AI, and verification must check substance as well as citation existence. They see continuing need for expert librarians and vendor scrutiny. Finally, Lambert argues that organizational structures and culture leave a widening gap between technical possibilities and practical implementation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists predominantly of conference presentations, practitioner anecdotes and the hosts' professional observations; quantitative examples are reported without underlying methods or independent validation.
pts.d: The document is Lambert and Gebauer's recap of the Texas Trailblazers conference, not a primary empirical study. Schwartz's survey example supplies a concrete quoted price reduction, but no quality assessment, measured labor time or generalizable sample. Lambert's suggestion that the work probably took half or less of the time is his inference. The Phillips 66 account attributes extraction and savings claims to its presenter, named in the transcript as Michael seen us; Lambert recalls more than 250,000 rights-of-way documents and savings well over $1 million. His conclusion that the work probably would not previously have been done is an interpretation, qualified by Gebauer's possibility of piecemeal work. The account does not explain whether the savings represent avoided hypothetical expenditure or reduced actual spending. Poole's intake example identifies tools and a zero project budget, but gives no accounting of existing licenses, staff time, performance or maintenance costs. Sikounis's upcoming Council Link report is the named quantitative basis for AFAs remaining around 10% and blended rate increases moving from approximately 3% before 2022 to 5% from about 2022 onward. The transcript does not provide the report's sample, denominator for the AFA share or full methodology, and it does not establish that AI caused those rate changes. John Risner of Filevine is reported to have conducted a deep examination of American case law and citator disagreement; the hosts report significant errors but provide no sample size or measured error rate. Gebauer mentions more than 800 hallucinated-case incidents and more than 100 in the US without identifying a tracker, reporting interval or denominator; these are incident-count claims, not benchmark hallucination rates. Pricing resistance, cognitive surrender, expanding skills and adoption barriers rely on observations, reported conversations and argument. The demand-expansion mechanism and 2027 disruption warning are predictions, not demonstrated market outcomes. Lambert also notes limited in-house-attorney participation, and Gebauer explicitly reports contradictory impressions of clients' adoption progress.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims concern current practice in 2026; explicit forward-looking horizons include pricing changes over the next few years and a 2027 disruption warning, with adoption and economic effects dependent on organizational choices.
pts.d: The hosts deliberately emphasize what is happening now rather than forecasting six to twelve months ahead. The three operational examples are presented as already implemented or experienced by the time of the conference. Poe's pricing shift is explicitly framed as beginning in 2026 and continuing forward; Lambert expects competing firm and client pricing interests to play out over the next couple of years. Sikounis's possible normalization of rate increases of 7% or more responds to a question about two or three years ahead and is conditional on 5% becoming normalized. Gorlick's warning names 2027 but offers no detailed forecast or probability. Associate-hiring reductions over the next few years are raised as a question, not a settled prediction. Additional demand is conditional on lowering cost and turnaround time and on clients wanting more work; it is not asserted to necessarily offset labor displacement. The survey reduction depended on explicit client permission to use AI, whereas some other clients reportedly prohibited it. Gebauer allows that some tasks may still suit hourly billing. Human verification, governance, education and simplicity are described as requirements for responsible and practical adoption. Lambert expects avoiding cognitive surrender to become harder as tools improve. Legal-research automation is qualified by the need to validate citations and their substantive use; access to case law alone is not treated as a sufficient solution. The hosts urge immediate experimentation and communication because organizational change lags technical capability, while acknowledging uncertainty about clients' readiness and future market structure.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The discussion primarily concerns law firms and corporate legal buyers, including associates, partners, pricing teams, legal operations, librarians and software vendors; it does not establish public access-to-justice effects.
pts.d: Associates face tension between learning efficiency tools and preserving billable work, alongside uncertainty about future hiring. Partners and firm leaders face compensation, staffing, adoption and revenue-model decisions. Pricing professionals on both provider and buyer sides must decide how gains from reduced production time are distributed and what outcomes or speed are worth. Corporate legal departments and general counsel are described as influential buyers able to authorize AI use, negotiate lower charges, request additional services or bring work in-house; the hosts caution that their actual progress is unevenly understood. Regulatory clients may obtain cheaper and more frequently updated multi-state surveys. Phillips 66's example concerns corporate risk visibility across rights-of-way documents, while Boomi's concerns internal intake operations. These are enterprise efficiency and scope-of-service examples, not claims about closing the civil justice gap. Legal operations and technology teams must manage integration, user-built applications, governance and adoption complexity. Practicing lawyers are expected to add client-business understanding and technological competence while retaining responsibility for context-sensitive judgment and verification. Law librarians retain an expert role in checking legal research and challenging vendor claims. Legal-AI vendors, including Harvey and Legora, face expanding expectations and research-market competition; their product activities are distinct from delivering legal work as an ALSP. The source does not quantify impacts by firm size, legal specialty beyond the examples, or demographic group.
